# Repositioning Strategy: From "Old" to "Original"

## A 30-Month Transition Plan to Recruit Under-35s Without Betraying the Base

---

## 0. How to Read This Document

Four things were asked for: **positioning**, **preserve/retire**, **channel and content**, **sequencing**. All four are here, plus the three things that determine whether they survive contact with the organisation: **governance** (which resolves the internal disagreement named in the brief), **measurement with a patience window**, and a **risk register with stop rules**.

The document is deliberately front-loaded on sequence and governance, because the brand's own history says that is where it failed — not on ambition or creative quality.

### 0.1 Assumptions, and the pre-work that gates the plan

This plan assumes a mass-market consumer brand with strong physical availability, a ~70-year history, an ageing loyalist skew, and two failed communications-led modernisation attempts. Five questions must be answered before money is committed, because the answers can redirect the strategy:

| # | Question to answer | Method | Time / indicative cost | What it gates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Is the under-35 problem perception or availability?** Cohort decline is frequently structural — wrong pack sizes, wrong entry price, absent from convenience/quick-commerce/marketplaces, absent from the occasions the cohort has. | Demand-space / category-entry-point study; panel data decomposition (penetration vs. frequency vs. weight by cohort); channel share vs. category by cohort | 8–10 weeks; mid-five-figure to low-six-figure | Whether this is a distribution/format plan with a comms layer, or a positioning plan. If the brand is absent from the occasion, tone of voice cannot fix it. |
| 2 | **What are loyalists actually attached to?** | Qual with 20–30 heavy buyers; sensory/product-experience probing; CRM churn analysis | 4–6 weeks; low-five-figure | The Immutables list (§4) and the wording of the product commitment (§5.2) |
| 3 | **Which brand assets are distinctive?** Fame × uniqueness for name, wordmark, colour, shape, mascot, sonic cue, tagline, pack architecture — tested in *both* cohorts | Distinctive-asset grid survey, n≥1,000 per cohort | 4 weeks; low-five-figure | Preserve / evolve / retire decisions. Internal taste is not admissible evidence. |
| 4 | **Is the durability/consistency territory available and safe?** | Competitive claim-and-asset audit (§2.3) + category norms review + regulatory/nutritional/materials review | 6 weeks; low-five-figure | Whether we run Route A or a fallback route (§2.4) |
| 5 | **Can we survive transparency?** | Internal disclosure audit — sourcing, plants, offshoring history, prior reformulations, labour and environmental exposure, litigation | 8–12 weeks; legal + supply chain led | Whether the proof agenda leads with spec transparency or with something else (§5.1) |

**Total pre-work window: ~12 weeks, run in parallel.** No external activity before it completes. This is Phase 0 in §7.

### 0.2 The load-bearing insight

> Loyalists fear **product** change. Under-35s reject **borrowed** communication. Therefore: hold the product sacred and take the risk in behaviour, evidence and distribution — not in claims.
>
> **Change what the brand *does* before you change what it *says*.**

---

## 1. Diagnosis: Why the Previous Attempts Failed

| What was done | Why it backfired |
|---|---|
| Made "youth" the target and "modern" the message | Announced the brand's own insecurity. Effort read as evidence of irrelevance. |
| Borrowed cultural codes (slang, memes, aesthetics) the brand had no claim to | Unearned codes read as costume. The brand became a punchline for the audience it courted. |
| Implicitly repudiated the heritage ("not your dad's X") | Told the loyal base *they* were the problem. Repudiation — not change — is what alienates a base. |
| Led with advertising because it is fast and controllable | No product, pack, channel or service change sat behind the claim. Nothing was checkable, so nothing was believable. |
| Ran it as a "relaunch" — one big reveal | A reveal creates a single high-contrast before/after that critics and loyalists can both attack, and a single date the trade press can anchor to. |

**Conclusion: the failure mode was sequence and sincerity, not ambition.** The brand tried to persuade before earning the right to be heard, and tried to buy a new identity rather than reveal an existing one.

**A consequence we must plan for, not ignore:** both campaigns are archived, searchable and will be resurfaced the moment the brand appears in earned media. See §8.4 for the response posture.

---

## 2. The Strategic Bet

### 2.1 The reframe

**Do not modernise the brand. Reframe its age from liability into proof.**

Seventy years is not a nostalgia asset; it is a *credibility* asset — but only when expressed as evidence rather than sentiment. The bridge to under-35s is not "we're young too." It is a small set of values this cohort demonstrably rewards and that a 70-year-old brand can claim more legitimately than any challenger:

- **Durability over disposability.** The cohort most exposed to fast, cheap, short-lived goods is receptive to things that last.
- **Consistency as integrity.** "Not cheapened to hit a price point" is a strong claim in a shrinkflation era.
- **Verifiability.** Real factories, real people, real records — showable, not assertable.
- **Anti-hype confidence.** Quiet competence reads as high status; visible trying reads as low status.
- **Rediscovery.** A heritage brand can be *found* rather than pitched — a stronger cultural mechanism than being sold.

Critically, **each of these also flatters the loyal base.** They are not asked to accept a new brand; they are told their long-standing judgment was right. That is the mechanism that dissolves the trade-off between the two audiences.

### 2.2 Target definition (and why 25–34 leads, not exclusively)

| Tier | Who | Role | Investment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary growth: 25–34 "quality-seeking pragmatists"** | Entering higher earning years, burned by disposable purchases, value-literate, research-driven, marketing-allergic | Carry near-term penetration and margin recovery. They have budget, replacement occasions and a bias toward evidence — the shortest path from our proof assets to purchase. | ~60% of growth-directed spend |
| **Early funnel: 18–24** | Category entrants, platform-native, status-sensitive | Deliberately *not* the persuasion target, but must not be abandoned — if 18–24 never enter, we rebuild this plan in 2035. Presence, not pursuit. | ~15% of growth-directed spend, mostly organic/social/collab/campus/entry formats |
| **Retention: existing base** | Heavy, older, high-loyalty | Reframed as *proof*, not legacy. The most persuasive asset we own. | ~25%, weighted to CRM, product commitment, service, availability |

The 25–34 lead is a bet, stated as such: it is the cohort where our credible propositions (durability, verifiability, price integrity) map onto real purchase decisions rather than identity signalling. If the demand-space work (Q1, §0.1) shows the lost occasions sit predominantly with 18–24, weightings invert and the collaboration/format agenda moves forward in the sequence.

### 2.3 Competitive audit — before the positioning is locked

"The original / the benchmark" is contested territory. Before committing, audit:

1. **Heritage-adjacent challengers** already using craft, provenance and durability codes — often smaller, more credible and faster.
2. **Private label** using craft cues at a lower price, which can neutralise "quality" as a differentiator.
3. **Revivalist / archival brands** that own "original" more sharply than a continuously-trading incumbent.
4. **Own-category norms:** is heritage a positive or a penalty in this category's shopper language?

Output: a claim-availability map (available / contested / occupied) and an asset-collision check (are our colours, shapes, typography already coded to a competitor?). If "original" is occupied, we take the adjacent ground: *"the standard"*, *"still made here"*, *"the one that gets repaired, not replaced."*

### 2.4 Route branch: what if durability/consistency is unavailable?

The Route A bet (unchanged specification, durability) is powerful in tools, footwear, denim, appliances, cookware, spirits. It is weak or actively harmful where the category expects innovation (beauty, snacks, personal tech, trend-led apparel), or where "unchanged since 1955" translates as high sugar/salt, legacy materials or pre-modern ingredient standards.

| Route | Trigger | Where heritage credibility rests | Core claim shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Consistency / durability** *(default)* | Spec is genuinely stable, defensible and reputationally clean | Product itself | "Made to the same standard since 19XX." |
| **B. Institutional knowledge** | Category expects innovation; spec has changed | 70 years of accumulated expertise — we innovate from a deeper base than anyone | "Seventy years of getting this wrong before we got it right. Which is why the new one works." |
| **C. Provenance & people** | Spec unremarkable; supply chain clean and ownable | Place, plant, tenured makers, method | "Same place. Same people. Same method." |
| **D. Service & stewardship** | Product parity; aftercare ownable | Repair, guarantee, availability of parts, lifetime relationship | "We're still here for the ones we sold in 1998." |
| **E. Community & continuity** | Strong subculture or user base | The users, across generations | "Nobody's first. Everybody's last." |

Route selection is a gate, not a preference — decided at the end of Phase 0 on the evidence from Q4 and Q5 (§0.1). Routes B–E use the *same* architecture that follows: same governance, same sequence, same one-message rule. Only the proof assets and claim change.

---

## 3. The New Positioning (Route A shown)

### 3.1 Positioning statement

> For people tired of things that don't last and brands that don't mean it, **[Brand]** is the original **[category]** — built to the same specification since 19XX, because we've never cheapened it to hit a price.

*(Removed from the earlier draft: "the one the newest ones are copying." It is unprovable, defensive in tone, and violates the anti-hype principle the strategy depends on. If competitive teardown evidence ever substantiates imitation, let third parties say it — never the brand.)*

### 3.2 Components

| Element | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frame of reference** | From "the traditional option in [category]" → "the benchmark in [category]" |
| **Point of difference** | Uninterrupted standard. Dated, specified, verifiable. |
| **Reasons to believe** | (1) Published specification with unchanged-since date; (2) named facilities, tenured makers, documented process; (3) longevity evidence — durability data, guarantee terms, multi-decade users; (4) price-integrity record |
| **Internal brand idea** | **"Old enough to know better."** *Internal only.* It carries a parental register that would patronise under-35s if it leaked. Enforcement: it appears in the brand book and briefs, never in a deck shown to media/agency talent, never in creative. Consumer-facing equivalents are drawn from the alternates below. |
| **Consumer-facing lines for testing** | "Still Made Right." / "Nothing New Since 19XX." / "Proof, Not Promises." / "The Standard." |
| **Tone shift** | From warm, explanatory, reassuring → dry, specific, unhurried, confident; occasionally funny at its own expense, never at its customers'. Fewer adjectives, more numbers. Fewer promises, more receipts. |
| **Never say** | "New." "Reinvented." "For a new generation." "Not your parents' —." Anything that dates the *customer* rather than the *standard*. |

### 3.3 The one-message rule (primary anti-backlash mechanism)

Both audiences receive **the same substantive claim**, differentiated only by **channel, context and craft** — never by content.

Segmentation by media is invisible and safe. Segmentation by *claim* is what gets screenshotted side-by-side and destroys credibility. Operational test, applied at every asset approval: *could a 68-year-old loyalist and a 28-year-old prospect both see this without either feeling addressed at the other's expense?* If no, it does not ship.

---

## 4. Brand Asset Audit: Preserve / Evolve / Retire

**Governing principle: retire *behaviours and executions*, never *distinctive assets*.** Seventy years of memory structure is the brand's only unfair advantage. Modern-looking brands with weak mental availability lose to old-looking brands with strong mental availability.

### 4.1 PRESERVE — the Immutables (Tier 1: CEO + board sign-off to alter)

- Brand name and core wordmark structure
- Primary brand colour and its category ownership
- Hero product specification / formula / fit — **publicly committed as unchanged**, per §5.2
- Founding date and origin place as on-pack cues
- The signature sensory asset (pack shape, closure sound, texture, ritual) — whichever the asset test proves famous *and* unique
- The hero SKU's core price-value relationship
- The mascot/character *as a character*, where one exists and tests high

### 4.2 EVOLVE — same asset, contemporary craft (Tier 2: brand director sign-off)

| Asset | Direction |
|---|---|
| Logotype | **Redraw, don't redesign.** Spacing, weight, optical balance. It should look like a better *print* of the same logo. |
| Packaging | **Restore, don't restyle.** Strip accumulated 1990s–2010s clutter, sub-claims and starbursts; return to a hierarchy that lets founding-era assets breathe. The best design language is usually in the brand's own archive, not a trend deck. |
| Colour system | Keep the primary; build a disciplined secondary palette for range navigation. |
| Typography | Modern secondary type for digital legibility; heritage wordmark untouched. |
| Art direction | From staged and aspirational → documentary, material, close-up, process- and people-led. The factory, the hands, the wear, the 30-year-old unit still working. |
| Formats & pack architecture | Single-serve, trial sizes, multipacks, refills; formats fitting smaller households and mobile occasions (see pricing architecture, §6.2). |
| Materials & footprint | Refillability, repairability, recyclable substrates — framed as durability, not virtue. |
| Digital / CRM / DTC | From brochureware to useful: spec transparency, provenance lookup, repair and parts, subscription for consumables. |

### 4.3 RETIRE — quietly, by replacement (Tier 3: team-level, no announcement)

- Taglines older than a decade that no longer carry meaning — retired by *replacement over time*, never a farewell campaign
- The mascot's performance style and schtick — keep the character, retire the act
- Aspirational-family stock photography and lifestyle tropes
- "New and improved" and any claim implying previous versions were deficient
- Sponsorships and partnerships with no strategic fit — let them lapse, don't exit loudly
- Nostalgia-as-content: reunion ads, "remember when", anniversary sentimentality. Heritage functions as **evidence**, never as **feeling**.
- Any asset scoring low on both fame and uniqueness — that is cost, not equity

### 4.4 Resolving the contradiction: tail SKUs and range change

The earlier draft promised "additive, never subtractive" and then instructed delisting of sub-2% SKUs. That is incoherent, and dangerous: in heritage brands, tail SKUs are disproportionately where the loudest loyalists live. Corrected rule:

**The hero product and its experience are untouched. Range change is permitted, but only under the Discontinuation Protocol.**

| SKU type | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Hero SKU(s) | Immutable. No change to spec, size, price architecture or availability without Tier 1 sign-off. |
| Tail SKU, low volume, **low loyalist intensity** (no CRM concentration, no community mentions, no review defence) | Normal range…[truncated]

## 5. Proof Before Persuasion: The Substance Agenda

Nothing in this plan is a campaign until Phase 2. The first 6–9 months are spent creating things that are *true*, so that later communication is reportage rather than assertion.

**1. Radical spec transparency.** Publish the full specification, the unchanged-since date, the sourcing, the facilities. Where the brand has been quietly better than competitors, say so with numbers. This is the highest-leverage, lowest-cost move available to a heritage brand and it is almost never done.

**2. A durability/standard commitment.** Extended guarantee, free repair, lifetime replacement of a component, or a public "we will never reformulate the hero to hit a price" pledge with a defined governance mechanism. Make the abstract positioning legally and operationally binding. This converts a claim into an asset.

**3. Access engineering.** Entry price points and formats for lower-commitment trial; distribution in the channels the cohort actually uses (convenience, quick-commerce, relevant marketplaces, the right specialist retail); correct on-shelf and on-site merchandising in those channels.

**4. Occasion expansion.** Based on the demand-space work, extend the range into 1–2 occasions the cohort has and the brand currently doesn't serve. Line extensions carry the recruitment risk; the hero SKU carries the reassurance.

**5. Experience repair.** Fix the mundane, credibility-destroying gaps: mobile site speed, product pages, reviews, customer service response times, delivery, returns. Under-35s judge brand modernity through operational competence long before they judge it through advertising.

**6. Loyalist protection programme.** Before anything is public: a direct, non-marketing communication to the base — not a campaign, a letter. *"Here's what is changing. Here's what will never change. Here's our commitment on the product you buy."* Give them advance notice, first access, and a named channel for concerns. Loyalists who feel consulted defend you; loyalists who feel surprised organize against you.

### 6.1 Architecture: three tiers, one truth

| Tier | Role | Channels | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Earned / Credibility** (lead with this) | Let others make the case. Rediscovery, not pitch. | Creator partnerships with genuine practitioners (makers, chefs, tradespeople, mechanics, stylists, athletes — whoever the category's real experts are), niche editorial, Reddit/forums/Discord where the category is actually debated, PR on the transparency and durability news | Factory and process films. Teardown/comparison content. "Why it hasn't changed" explainers. Long-form provenance. Reviews and stress tests by people with nothing to gain. |
| **Owned / Depth** | Convert interest into understanding and purchase. | Brand site, YouTube long-form, TikTok/Reels/Shorts, newsletter, DTC, in-store | Process and craft series. ## 1. Diagnosis: Why the Previous Attempts Failed

| What was done | Why it backfired |
|---|---|
| Positioned "youth" as the target and "modern" as the message | Announced the brand's own insecurity. Under-35s read effort as evidence of irrelevance. |
| Borrowed cultural codes (slang, memes, aesthetics) the brand had no claim to | Unearned codes read as costume. The brand became a punchline for the very audience it courted. |
| Implicitly repudiated the heritage ("not your dad's X") | Told the loyal base they were the problem. Repudiation, not change, is what alienates a base. |
| Led with advertising because it's fast and controllable | There was no product, pack, channel, or experience change behind the claim. Nothing was checkable, so nothing was believable. |
| Ran the change as a "relaunch" — one big reveal | A reveal creates a single, high-contrast before/after that critics and loyalists can both attack. |

**Conclusion:** The failure mode was not ambition. It was *sequence* and *sincerity*. The brand tried to persuade before it had earned the right to be listened to, and it tried to buy a new identity rather than reveal an existing one.

---

## 2. The Strategic Bet

Seventy years is not a nostalgia asset; it is a *credibility* asset — but only if it's expressed as evidence rather than sentiment. The bridge to under-35s is not "we're young too." - **Insider knowledge.** "If you know, you know" — a heritage brand can be rediscovered, which is a far more powerful cultural mechanism than being pitched.

This is a live organisational problem in the brief and it is treated as background colour. A "change budget" concept with tiered decision rights (CEO-level immutables / brand-director-level evolutions / team-level executions) would have closed it — the ingredients are present in §4 but never assembled into governance.

---

## 2. Strategic weaknesses

**2.1 The positioning bet is category-contingent and no fallback is offered.** "Never reformulated, unchanged since 19XX, durability over disposability" is powerful for tools, footwear, denim, appliances, cookware, spirits. It is weak or actively harmful where the category expects innovation (beauty, snacks, personal tech, trend-led apparel), or where "unchanged formula" translates as "high sugar/salt, legacy materials, pre-modern ingredient standards." §0 flags category ambiguity, then §2–3 proceed as though the durability route is available. The plan needs a branch: if consistency/durability is unavailable or reputationally risky, where does heritage credibility rest instead (provenance, service, community, institutional knowledge)?

**2.2 "Radical spec transparency" is recommended without a pre-audit gate.** Publishing sourcing, facilities and specification invites scrutiny that a 70-year-old supply chain may not survive — offshoring, plant consolidation, ingredient substitutions already made, labour or environmental exposure. Transparency should be preceded by an internal disclosure audit with a go/no-go decision, and the plan should name what happens if the audit finds something unflattering.

**2.3 The "never reformulate" pledge is treated as pure upside.** Making a positioning "legally and operationally binding" also creates warranty/consumer-protection exposure, and removes flexibility against input shortages, regulatory reformulation mandates, and sustainability requirements. Carve-outs, governance wording, and legal review are needed; the doc presents only the benefit.

**2.4 Internal contradiction: "additive, never subtractive" vs. delisting tail SKUs.** §4 promises nothing is taken away, then instructs delisting of sub-2% SKUs. In heritage brands, tail SKUs are disproportionately where the most vocal loyalists live; "on a normal range-review cadence" is not protection, it is hoping nobody notices. Either exempt loyalist-favourite tails, or build a discontinuation protocol (advance notice, final-run availability, DTC-only continuation).

**2.5 Related tension unaddressed: line extensions ARE product change.** The plan holds the hero sacred but expands into 1–2 new occasions. Loyalists frequently read range extension as dilution and as a leading indicator of eventual hero change. The real backlash risk is *signal*, not subtraction, and the plan doesn't handle it. Needs explicit architecture (sub-brand? endorsed? separate naming?) and a stated reassurance mechanism at extension launch.

**2.6 The target narrowing to 25–34 is convenient and under-argued.** Deprioritising 18–24 is a defensible choice, but it is a major bet presented as a definition. If 18–24 never enter the franchise, the same cohort problem recurs in a decade, and the "quality-seeking pragmatist" segment is precisely the one competitors also chase. Needs an explicit rationale plus a low-cost early-funnel presence so the brand isn't rebuilding this plan in 2035.

**2.7 No competitive analysis.** "The original / the benchmark" is a contested space — heritage-adjacent challengers, private label with craft cues, and revivalist brands may already own durability or authenticity codes in this category. Without a competitive asset and claim audit, the positioning may be unavailable or already better executed by someone smaller and more credible.

**2.8 The reputation residue of the two failed campaigns is ignored.** Those campaigns are archived, searchable, and will resurface the moment the brand appears on Reddit, TikTok or in trade press — "remember when they tried to be cool." The earned-media-first strategy walks the brand into the most hostile terrain first with no plan for this. Needs a defined posture (acknowledge once, dryly; never re-litigate; brief creators and community managers on the response) and a decision on whether to pre-empt it.

**2.9 The creator strategy has an unresolved authenticity paradox.** Paid practitioner content is still paid, and this cohort is highly literate about disclosure. The plan needs: a no-strings seeding programme, tolerance for and public non-interference with negative reviews, a disclosure posture, and a rule that the most credible tier of proof is deliberately *not* bought. Otherwise "earned credibility" is just influencer marketing with better casting — which is exactly the trap that produced campaign #2.

---

## 3. Commercial and operational gaps

- **No budget shape.** No reallocation logic (what % shifts from paid to product, ops, earned), no payback expectation, no cost view on the durability guarantee, repair programme, or DTC build.
- **Pricing tension unresolved.** "Entry price points for trial" sits awkwardly against a positioning built on price integrity and never cheapening the product. Needs an architecture that separates trial format economics from hero-price signalling.
- **Trade and channel reality missing.** Entering quick-commerce, marketplaces and convenience requires buyer buy-in, listing economics, pack-format changes and creates channel conflict with existing key accounts — the brand's single strongest asset. There is no trade narrative, no sales-force story, no retailer value exchange ("what's the story for my shelf?").
- **Capability and resourcing absent.** Documentary content at volume, fast community response, repair operations, spec-transparency infrastructure are all new muscles. No in-house/agency model, content velocity assumption, or hiring implication.
- **No internal launch plan.** The brief's internal disagreement extends to frontline and retail staff; staff cynicism leaks and undermines authenticity faster than advertising does. Employee-led content is proposed (§6.1) without the internal engagement work that makes it possible.
- **No risk register.** Failure modes (loyalist backlash resurgence, creator misfire, transparency exposure, competitor co-option of "original," leadership change) with pre-agreed responses, a social-listening baseline, and a defined pause threshold.

---

- **"This single rule removes ~80% of backlash risk"** is an invented number in a document that preaches "numbers over adjectives." Remove or substantiate. Same for "almost never done" and "in almost every case."

- **"Old enough to know better"** is a strong internal idea but carries a parental/wisdom register that would patronise under-35s if it ever leaked outward. Flag it as internal-only with enforcement, or pressure-test it.
- **Proportion problem.** Roughly two-thirds of the length goes to positioning and the asset audit; execution, sequencing, governance and measurement — the areas where the brand has already failed twice — get the least. Tighten the overlap between §2, §3.2 and §6.2 to fund the missing sections.
- **§0 is good practice** (naming what must be verified) but stops short of committing to a research plan: methods, timeline, cost, and which decisions are gated on which findings.

---

## 5. Prioritised fix list

1. Complete §6.3 and add the missing **sequencing/phasing plan** — phases, activities, gate criteria to advance, what is deliberately withheld until later, and the point of irreversibility.
2. Add a **measurement and patience framework**, including leading indicators by cohort, loyalist-health metrics, and an explicit "what we will not judge this on in year one."
3. Add a **governance and change-absorption mechanism** that resolves the internal disagreement: decision rights by asset tier, a defined change budget, tripwires and stop rules.
4. Add a **risk register with kill-switches**, a social-listening baseline, and a defined backlash-response protocol.
5. Insert a **transparency pre-audit gate** and legal carve-outs on the never-reformulate pledge.
6. Resolve the **additive-vs-delisting** contradiction and the **line-extension signalling** risk.
7. Add **commercial substance**: budget reallocation, pricing architecture, trade narrative, capability/resourcing.
8. Add a **competitive audit** and a **fallback positioning branch** if durability/consistency proves unavailable in this category.
9. Add an **internal/employee engagement plan** ahead of any external activity.
10. Strip unsupported quantifications and the unprovable "they're copying us" claim.

---

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**

*(Rationale: the thinking is strong and much of it is reusable, but the document is literally incomplete, omits one of the four explicitly requested deliverables — the one its own diagnosis identifies as the root cause of prior failure — and leaves the brief's stated internal-alignment problem unaddressed, along with measurement, risk and commercial substance.)*

Critically, **every one of these propositions also flatters the loyal base.** They are not asked to accept a new brand; they are told their long-standing judgment was right. This is the mechanism that removes the trade-off between the two audiences.

## 3. The New Positioning

### 3.1 Positioning statement

> For people who are tired of things that don't last and brands that don't mean it, **[Brand]** is the original **[category]** — made to the same standard since 19XX, because we've never had to change it to make it cheaper. Not the newest. The one the newest ones are copying.

### 3.2 Components

| Element | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Primary growth target** | 25–34 "quality-seeking pragmatists": entering higher earning years, burned by disposable purchases, value-literate, research-driven, allergic to marketing. Not "Gen Z" as an aesthetic. |
| **Retention target** | The existing base, reframed as *proof*, not as legacy. They are the brand's most compelling asset, not its constraint. |
| **Frame of reference** | Move from "the traditional option in [category]" to "the benchmark in [category]" — the standard against which new entrants are measured. |
| **Point of difference** | Uninterrupted standard. Verifiable, dated, specific. |
| **Reasons to believe** | (1) Published, unchanged specification/formula; (2) named facilities, tenured makers, real process; (3) longevity/performance evidence — durability data, guarantees, multi-decade users; (4) price-integrity record. |
| **Brand idea (internal)** | **"Old enough to know better."** |
| **Alternates for testing** | "The Original Doesn't Need Updating." / "Still Made Right." / "Nothing New Since 19XX." / "Proof, Not Promises." |
| **Tone shift** | From *warm, explanatory, reassuring* → to *dry, confident, specific, unhurried, occasionally funny at its own expense — never at its customers' expense.* Fewer adjectives, more numbers. Fewer promises, more receipts. |
| **What we will never say** | "New." "Reinvented." "For a new generation." "Not your parents' —." Anything that dates the brand's *customers* rather than the brand's *standard*. |

### 3.3 The one-message rule (anti-backlash mechanism)

Both audiences receive **the same substantive claim**, differentiated only by **channel, context, and craft** — never by content. Segmentation by media is invisible and safe. Segmentation by *claim* is the thing that gets screenshotted side by side and destroys credibility. Write every asset so that a loyalist and a 28-year-old could both see it without either feeling addressed at the other's expense.

## 4. Brand Asset Audit: Preserve / Evolve / Retire

**Governing principle: retire *behaviours and executions*, never *distinctive assets*.** Seventy years of memory structure is the only unfair advantage the brand has. Modern-looking brands with no mental availability lose to old-looking brands with plenty of it.

### PRESERVE — the Immutables (require CEO sign-off to alter)

- Brand name and core wordmark structure
- Primary brand colour and its ownership
- Hero product formula / specification / fit — **explicitly guaranteed unchanged, in writing, publicly**
- Founding date and origin place as on-pack cues
- The signature sensory asset (pack shape, closure sound, texture, ritual) — whatever the asset test proves is famous *and* unique
- The core price-value relationship on the hero SKU
- The mascot/character *as a character*, if one exists and tests high

### EVOLVE — same asset, contemporary craft

| Asset | Direction |
|---|---|
| Logotype | Redraw, don't redesign. Correct spacing, weight, optical balance. It should look like a better print of the same logo, not a new one. |
| Packaging | Restore, don't restyle. Strip accumulated 1990s–2010s clutter, sub-claims, and starbursts; return to a cleaner hierarchy that lets the founding-era assets breathe. Most heritage brands' best design language is in their own archive, not in a trend deck. |
| Colour system | Keep the primary; build a disciplined secondary palette for range navigation. |
| Typography | Modern secondary type system for digital legibility; heritage wordmark untouched. |
| Photography/art direction | From staged, aspirational, lit-to-perfection → to documentary, material, close-up, process- and people-led. Show the factory, the hands, the wear, the 30-year-old unit still working. |
| Tone of voice | Per §3.2. |
| Pack architecture & formats | Single-serve, trial sizes, multipacks, refills, formats fitting smaller households and mobile occasions. |
| Materials & footprint | Refillability, repairability, recyclable substrates — framed as durability, not virtue. |
| Digital/CRM/DTC | From brochureware to genuinely useful: spec transparency, provenance lookup, repair/replacement, subscription for consumables. |

### RETIRE — quietly, with no announcement

- Any tagline older than a decade that no longer means anything (retire by *replacement over time*, not by farewell campaign)
- The performance style of the mascot, not the mascot: keep the character, retire the schtick
- Aspirational-family stock photography and "lifestyle" tropes
- "New and improved" and any claim that implies previous versions were deficient
- Tail sub-brands and SKUs contributing under a defined threshold (e.g. <2% of revenue with no strategic role) — delist on a normal range-review cadence, not as a "streamlining" story
- Sponsorships and partnerships with no strategic fit (let them lapse; don't exit loudly)
- Nostalgia-as-content: reunion ads, "remember when," anniversary sentimentality. Heritage must function as *evidence*, never as *feeling*.
- Any asset that tests low on both fame and uniqueness — these are cost, not equity

**The rule that protects the base: additive, never subtractive.** New audiences get new formats, new occasions, new collaborations, new channels — the hero product and its experience are untouched. Nobody's product gets taken away or "improved." This single rule removes ~80% of backlash risk.

## 5. Proof Before Persuasion: The Substance Agenda

Nothing in this plan is a campaign until Phase 2. The first 6–9 months are spent creating things that are *true*, so that later communication is reportage rather than assertion.

**1. Radical spec transparency.** Publish the full specification, the unchanged-since date, the sourcing, the facilities. Where the brand has been quietly better than competitors, say so with numbers. This is the highest-leverage, lowest-cost move available to a heritage brand and it is almost never done.

**2. A durability/standard commitment.** Extended guarantee, free repair, lifetime replacement of a component, or a public "we will never reformulate the hero to hit a price" pledge with a defined governance mechanism. Make the abstract positioning legally and operationally binding. This converts a claim into an asset.

**3. Access engineering.** Entry price points and formats for lower-commitment trial; distribution in the channels the cohort actually uses (convenience, quick-commerce, relevant marketplaces, the right specialist retail); correct on-shelf and on-site merchandising in those channels.

**4. Occasion expansion.** Based on the demand-space work, extend the range into 1–2 occasions the cohort has and the brand currently doesn't serve. Line extensions carry the recruitment risk; the hero SKU carries the reassurance.

**5. Experience repair.** Fix the mundane, credibility-destroying gaps: mobile site speed, product pages, reviews, customer service response times, delivery, returns. Under-35s judge brand modernity through operational competence long before they judge it through advertising.

**6. Loyalist protection programme.** Before anything is public: a direct, non-marketing communication to the base — not a campaign, a letter. *"Here's what is changing. Here's what will never change. Here's our commitment on the product you buy."* Give them advance notice, first access, and a named channel for concerns. Loyalists who feel consulted defend you; loyalists who feel surprised organize against you.

### 6.2 Content principles

- **Show the making.** Process content is the single most reliable credibility engine available to a heritage manufacturer and it plays natively on the platforms under-35s use.

# Critique: "From 'Old' to 'Original'" Repositioning Strategy

## Summary judgment

The thinking that exists is above-average — the diagnosis of the prior failures, the "retire behaviours, never distinctive assets" rule, the one-message rule, and the proof-before-persuasion sequence logic are genuinely strong and would survive contact with a real client. But the document **fails as a deliverable**: it terminates mid-sentence, and the single requirement the brief emphasised most — *how to sequence the transition* — is never delivered. A strategy whose own diagnosis is "the failure mode was sequence, not ambition" and which then omits the sequence is self-refuting.

---

## 1. Deliverable failures (must fix before anything else)

**1.1 The output is truncated.** It ends at "Collaborations are the high—". Section 6.3 is incomplete and everything after it is absent.

**1.2 The sequencing requirement is missing.** The brief asked for four things: positioning, preserve/retire, channel and content, **and sequencing**. Three are delivered; the fourth exists only as fragments ("30-Month Plan" in the subtitle, "first 6–9 months," "nothing is a campaign until Phase 2"). There is no phase map, no milestones, no gate criteria for advancing from phase to phase, no view of what happens in months 18–30, and no defined "point of no return." This is the section that would actually have prevented backlash #3.

**1.3 No measurement framework.** There is no way to know whether the plan is working, and — more dangerous for a heritage brand — **no stated patience window**. Repositioning of this type produces lagging commercial results and a leading-indicator profile (asset recognition, salience by cohort, trial rate among 25–34, penetration, loyalist retention/defection, sentiment mix, share of category entry points). Without a pre-agreed "here is what we will *not* judge this on in year one," the internal sceptics identified in the brief will kill the plan at month nine and force campaign #3.

**1.4 The internal disagreement is never resolved.** The brief explicitly states that "internal teams disagree on how much change the brand can absorb." The document answers this implicitly ("hold the product sacred") but provides no mechanism: no change-absorption framework, no decision rights, no escalation path, no pre-agreed tripwires or stop rules, no shared metric that lets both the conservative and the aggressive camp be partially right. This is a live organisational problem in the brief and it is treated as background colour. A "change budget" concept with tiered decision rights (CEO-level immutables / brand-director-level evolutions / team-level executions) would have closed it — the ingredients are present in §4 but never assembled into governance.

---

## 2. Strategic weaknesses

**2.1 The positioning bet is category-contingent and no fallback is offered.** "Never reformulated, unchanged since 19XX, durability over disposability" is powerful for tools, footwear, denim, appliances, cookware, spirits. It is weak or actively harmful where the category expects innovation (beauty, snacks, personal tech, trend-led apparel), or where "unchanged formula" translates as "high sugar/salt, legacy materials, pre-modern ingredient standards." §0 flags category ambiguity, then §2–3 proceed as though the durability route is available. The plan needs a branch: if consistency/durability is unavailable or reputationally risky, where does heritage credibility rest instead (provenance, service, community, institutional knowledge)?

**2.2 "Radical spec transparency" is recommended without a pre-audit gate.** Publishing sourcing, facilities and specification invites scrutiny that a 70-year-old supply chain may not survive — offshoring, plant consolidation, ingredient substitutions already made, labour or environmental exposure. Transparency should be preceded by an internal disclosure audit with a go/no-go decision, and the plan should name what happens if the audit finds something unflattering.

**2.3 The "never reformulate" pledge is treated as pure upside.** Making a positioning "legally and operationally binding" also creates warranty/consumer-protection exposure, and removes flexibility against input shortages, regulatory reformulation mandates, and sustainability requirements. Carve-outs, governance wording, and legal review are needed; the doc presents only the benefit.

**2.4 Internal contradiction: "additive, never subtractive" vs. delisting tail SKUs.** §4 promises nothing is taken away, then instructs delisting of sub-2% SKUs. In heritage brands, tail SKUs are disproportionately where the most vocal loyalists live; "on a normal range-review cadence" is not protection, it is hoping nobody notices. Either exempt loyalist-favourite tails, or build a discontinuation protocol (advance notice, final-run availability, DTC-only continuation).

**2.5 Related tension unaddressed: line extensions ARE product change.** The plan holds the hero sacred but expands into 1–2 new occasions. Loyalists frequently read range extension as dilution and as a leading indicator of eventual hero change. The real backlash risk is *signal*, not subtraction, and the plan doesn't handle it. Needs explicit architecture (sub-brand? endorsed? separate naming?) and a stated reassurance mechanism at extension launch.

**2.6 The target narrowing to 25–34 is convenient and under-argued.** Deprioritising 18–24 is a defensible choice, but it is a major bet presented as a definition. If 18–24 never enter the franchise, the same cohort problem recurs in a decade, and the "quality-seeking pragmatist" segment is precisely the one competitors also chase. Needs an explicit rationale plus a low-cost early-funnel presence so the brand isn't rebuilding this plan in 2035.

**2.7 No competitive analysis.** "The original / the benchmark" is a contested space — heritage-adjacent challengers, private label with craft cues, and revivalist brands may already own durability or authenticity codes in this category. Without a competitive asset and claim audit, the positioning may be unavailable or already better executed by someone smaller and more credible.

**2.8 The reputation residue of the two failed campaigns is ignored.** Those campaigns are archived, searchable, and will resurface the moment the brand appears on Reddit, TikTok or in trade press — "remember when they tried to be cool." The earned-media-first strategy walks the brand into the most hostile terrain first with no plan for this. Needs a defined posture (acknowledge once, dryly; never re-litigate; brief creators and community managers on the response) and a decision on whether to pre-empt it.

**2.9 The creator strategy has an unresolved authenticity paradox.** Paid practitioner content is still paid, and this cohort is highly literate about disclosure. The plan needs: a no-strings seeding programme, tolerance for and public non-interference with negative reviews, a disclosure posture, and a rule that the most credible tier of proof is deliberately *not* bought. Otherwise "earned credibility" is just influencer marketing with better casting — which is exactly the trap that produced campaign #2.

**2.10 The loyalist letter may manufacture the anxiety it aims to prevent.** Telling a base that hasn't noticed anything "here's what is changing" creates a change narrative, and hands trade press a story. Better: segment to highest-value/most-engaged loyalists via CRM, frame as *commitment* (what will never change) rather than *change notice*, and treat it as a listening exercise rather than an announcement.

## 3. Commercial and operational gaps

- **No budget shape.** No reallocation logic (what % shifts from paid to product, ops, earned), no payback expectation, no cost view on the durability guarantee, repair programme, or DTC build.

## 1. Diagnosis: Why the Previous Attempts Failed

| What was done | Why it backfired |
|---|---|
| Made "youth" the target and "modern" the message | Announced the brand's own insecurity. Effort read as evidence of irrelevance. |
| Borrowed cultural codes (slang, memes, aesthetics) the brand had no claim to | Unearned codes read as costume. The brand became a punchline for the audience it courted. |
| Implicitly repudiated the heritage ("not your dad's X") | Told the loyal base *they* were the problem. Repudiation — not change — is what alienates a base. |
| Led with advertising because it is fast and controllable | No product, pack, channel or service change sat behind the claim. Nothing was checkable, so nothing was believable. |
| Ran it as a "relaunch" — one big reveal | A reveal creates a single high-contrast before/after that critics and loyalists can both attack, and a single date the trade press can anchor to. |

**Conclusion: the failure mode was sequence and sincerity, not ambition.** The brand tried to persuade before earning the right to be heard, and tried to buy a new identity rather than reveal an existing one.

**A consequence we must plan for, not ignore:** both campaigns are archived, searchable and will be resurfaced the moment the brand appears in earned media. See §8.4 for the response posture.

## 2. The Strategic Bet

### 2.1 The reframe

**Do not modernise the brand. Reframe its age from liability into proof.**

Seventy years is not a nostalgia asset; it is a *credibility* asset — but only when expressed as evidence rather than sentiment. The bridge to under-35s is not "we're young too." It is a small set of values this cohort demonstrably rewards and that a 70-year-old brand can claim more legitimately than any challenger:

- **Durability over disposability.** The cohort most exposed to fast, cheap, short-lived goods is receptive to things that last.
- **Consistency as integrity.** "Not cheapened to hit a price point" is a strong claim in a shrinkflation era.
- **Verifiability.** Real factories, real people, real records — showable, not assertable.
- **Anti-hype confidence.** Quiet competence reads as high status; visible trying reads as low status.
- **Rediscovery.** A heritage brand can be *found* rather than pitched — a stronger cultural mechanism than being sold.

Critically, **each of these also flatters the loyal base.** They are not asked to accept a new brand; they are told their long-standing judgment was right. That is the mechanism that dissolves the trade-off between the two audiences.

### 2.2 Target definition (and why 25–34 leads, not exclusively)

| Tier | Who | Role | Investment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary growth: 25–34 "quality-seeking pragmatists"** | Entering higher earning years, burned by disposable purchases, value-literate, research-driven, marketing-allergic | Carry near-term penetration and margin recovery. They have budget, replacement occasions and a bias toward evidence — the shortest path from our proof assets to purchase. | ~60% of growth-directed spend |
| **Early funnel: 18–24** | Category entrants, platform-native, status-sensitive | Deliberately *not* the persuasion target, but must not be abandoned — if 18–24 never enter, we rebuild this plan in 2035. Presence, not pursuit. | ~15% of growth-directed spend, mostly organic/social/collab/campus/entry formats |
| **Retention: existing base** | Heavy, older, high-loyalty | Reframed as *proof*, not legacy. The most persuasive asset we own. | ~25%, weighted to CRM, product commitment, service, availability |

The 25–34 lead is a bet, stated as such: it is the cohort where our credible propositions (durability, verifiability, price integrity) map onto real purchase decisions rather than identity signalling. If the demand-space work (Q1, §0.1) shows the lost occasions sit predominantly with 18–24, weightings invert and the collaboration/format agenda moves forward in the sequence.

### 2.3 Competitive audit — before the positioning is locked

"The original / the benchmark" is contested territory. Before committing, audit:

1. **Heritage-adjacent challengers** already using craft, provenance and durability codes — often smaller, more credible and faster.
2. **Private label** using craft cues at a lower price, which can neutralise "quality" as a differentiator.
3. **Revivalist / archival brands** that own "original" more sharply than a continuously-trading incumbent.
4. **Own-category norms:** is heritage a positive or a penalty in this category's shopper language?

Output: a claim-availability map (available / contested / occupied) and an asset-collision check (are our colours, shapes, typography already coded to a competitor?). If "original" is occupied, we take the adjacent ground: *"the standard"*, *"still made here"*, *"the one that gets repaired, not replaced."*

### 2.4 Route branch: what if durability/consistency is unavailable?

The Route A bet (unchanged specification, durability) is powerful in tools, footwear, denim, appliances, cookware, spirits. It is weak or actively harmful where the category expects innovation (beauty, snacks, personal tech, trend-led apparel), or where "unchanged since 1955" translates as high sugar/salt, legacy materials or pre-modern ingredient standards.

| Route | Trigger | Where heritage credibility rests | Core claim shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Consistency / durability** *(default)* | Spec is genuinely stable, defensible and reputationally clean | Product itself | "Made to the same standard since 19XX." |
| **B. Institutional knowledge** | Category expects innovation; spec has changed | 70 years of accumulated expertise — we innovate from a deeper base than anyone | "Seventy years of getting this wrong before we got it right. Which is why the new one works." |
| **C. Provenance & people** | Spec unremarkable; supply chain clean and ownable | Place, plant, tenured makers, method | "Same place. Same people. Same method." |
| **D. Service & stewardship** | Product parity; aftercare ownable | Repair, guarantee, availability of parts, lifetime relationship | "We're still here for the ones we sold in 1998." |
| **E. Community & continuity** | Strong subculture or user base | The users, across generations | "Nobody's first. Everybody's last." |

Route selection is a gate, not a preference — decided at the end of Phase 0 on the evidence from Q4 and Q5 (§0.1). Routes B–E use the *same* architecture that follows: same governance, same sequence, same one-message rule. Only the proof assets and claim change.

| **Point of difference** | Uninterrupted standard. Dated, specified, verifiable. |
| **Reasons to believe** | (1) Published specification with unchanged-since date; (2) named facilities, tenured makers, documented process; (3) longevity evidence — durability data, guarantee terms, multi-decade users; (4) price-integrity record |
| **Internal brand idea** | **"Old enough to know better."** *Internal only.* It carries a parental register that would patronise under-35s if it leaked. Enforcement: it appears in the brand book and briefs, never in a deck shown to media/agency talent, never in creative. Consumer-facing equivalents are drawn from the alternates below. |
| **Consumer-facing lines for testing** | "Still Made Right." / "Nothing New Since 19XX." / "Proof, Not Promises." / "The Standard." |
| **Tone shift** | From warm, explanatory, reassuring → dry, specific, unhurried, confident; occasionally funny at its own expense, never at its customers'. Fewer adjectives, more numbers. Fewer promises, more receipts. |
| **Never say** | "New." "Reinvented." "For a new generation." "Not your parents' —." Anything that dates the *customer* rather than the *standard*. |

### 3.3 The one-message rule (primary anti-backlash mechanism)

Both audiences receive **the same substantive claim**, differentiated only by **channel, context and craft** — never by content.

Segmentation by media is invisible and safe. Segmentation by *claim* is what gets screenshotted side-by-side and destroys credibility. Operational test, applied at every asset approval: *could a 68-year-old loyalist and a 28-year-old prospect both see this without either feeling addressed at the other's expense?* If no, it does not ship.

---

## 4. Brand Asset Audit: Preserve / Evolve / Retire

**Governing principle: retire *behaviours and executions*, never *distinctive assets*.** Seventy years of memory structure is the brand's only unfair advantage. Modern-looking brands with weak mental availability lose to old-looking brands with strong mental availability.

### 4.1 PRESERVE — the Immutables (Tier 1: CEO + board sign-off to alter)

- Brand name and core wordmark structure
- Primary brand colour and its category ownership
- Hero product specification / formula / fit — **publicly committed as unchanged**, per §5.2
- Founding date and origin place as on-pack cues
- The signature sensory asset (pack shape, closure sound, texture, ritual) — whichever the asset test proves famous *and* unique
- The hero SKU's core price-value relationship
- The mascot/character *as a character*, where one exists and tests high

### 4.2 EVOLVE — same asset, contemporary craft (Tier 2: brand director sign-off)

| Asset | Direction |
|---|---|
| Logotype | **Redraw, don't redesign.** Spacing, weight, optical balance. It should look like a better *print* of the same logo. |
| Packaging | **Restore, don't restyle.** Strip accumulated 1990s–2010s clutter, sub-claims and starbursts; return to a hierarchy that lets founding-era assets breathe. The best design language is usually in the brand's own archive, not a trend deck. |
| Colour system | Keep the primary; build a disciplined secondary palette for range navigation. |
| Typography | Modern secondary type for digital legibility; heritage wordmark untouched. |
| Art direction | From staged and aspirational → documentary, material, close-up, process- and people-led. The factory, the hands, the wear, the 30-year-old unit still working. |
| Formats & pack architecture | Single-serve, trial sizes, multipacks, refills; formats fitting smaller households and mobile occasions (see pricing architecture, §6.2). |
| Materials & footprint | Refillability, repairability, recyclable substrates — framed as durability, not virtue. |
| Digital / CRM / DTC | From brochureware to useful: spec transparency, provenance lookup, repair and parts, subscription for consumables. |

### 4.3 RETIRE — quietly, by replacement (Tier 3: team-level, no announcement)

- Taglines older than a decade that no longer carry meaning — retired by *replacement over time*, never a farewell campaign
- The mascot's performance style and schtick — keep the character, retire the act
- Aspirational-family stock photography and lifestyle tropes
- "New and improved" and any claim implying previous versions were deficient
- Sponsorships and partnerships with no strategic fit — let them lapse, don't exit loudly
- Nostalgia-as-content: reunion ads, "remember when", anniversary sentimentality. Heritage functions as **evidence**, never as **feeling**.
- Any asset scoring low on both fame and uniqueness — that is cost, not equity

### 4.4 Resolving the contradiction: tail SKUs and range change

The earlier draft promised "additive, never subtractive" and then instructed delisting of sub-2% SKUs. That is incoherent, and dangerous: in heritage brands, tail SKUs are disproportionately where the loudest loyalists live. Corrected rule:

**The hero product and its experience are untouched. Range change is permitted, but only under the Discontinuation Protocol.**

| SKU type | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Hero SKU(s) | Immutable. No change to spec, size, price architecture or availability without Tier 1 sign-off. |
| Tail SKU, low volume, **low loyalist intensity** (no CRM concentration, no community mentions, no review defence) | Normal range review. Delist quietly. |
| Tail SKU, low volume, **high loyalist intensity** (concentrated in CRM heavy buyers, defended in reviews/forums) | Do **not** delist on volume alone. Options in order of preference: (a) keep as a deliberate loyalty cost, booked as retention spend not gross margin; (b) migrate to DTC-only continuous availability; (c) annual final-run with 6 months' notice and named contact for the affected base. |
| Any delist touching >0.5% of identified heavy buyers | 90 days' advance notice via CRM, stock-up window, explicit statement that the hero is unaffected, and a route to raise objections that a human answers. |

**Test before delisting:** loyalist intensity index = share of SKU volume from top-decile CRM buyers × mention frequency in owned reviews/social. Volume alone is not a decision input.

### 4.5 Line extensions ARE product change — architecture and reassurance

Loyalists frequently read range extension as dilution, and as a leading indicator of eventual hero change. The risk is **signal**, not subtraction. Rules:

1. **Endorsed architecture, not masterbrand stretch.** New occasions launch as *[Brand] [Descriptor]* — clearly endorsed, clearly separate, never as a variant of the hero. No "[Brand] 2.0", no numerals on the hero, no "Original" retro-label on the hero (retro-labelling the hero is the classic error: it recodes the hero as one option among several).
2. **The hero is never repackaged in the same wave as an extension.** Minimum six months' separation, so no shopper sees hero change and range change together.
3. **Reassurance at launch, in the same breath:** every extension announcement carries the sentence "[Hero] is unchanged, and will stay that way," with a link to the published spec and commitment.
4. **Extensions carry recruitment risk; the hero carries reassurance.** If an extension fails, it is withdrawn without narrative consequence for the hero — which is precisely why it must be architecturally separate.

---

## 5. Proof Before Persuasion: The Substance Agenda

Nothing here is a campaign. These are the assets that make later communication *reportage* rather than assertion. They run in Phases 1–2 (§7).

### 5.1 Spec transparency — gated, not automatic

Publishing specification, sourcing and facilities is the highest-leverage move available to a heritage manufacturer. It is also an invitation to scrutiny that a 70-year supply chain may not survive.

**Mandatory pre-audit (Phase 0, Q5).** Legal + supply chain + comms review of: offshoring history, plant closures, prior reformulations, ingredient substitutions, labour and environmental exposure, supplier audit gaps, live litigation.

| Audit finding | Decision |
|---|---|
| Clean and better-than-category | **Go.** Lead the proof agenda with full transparency, including numbers and named facilities. |
| Clean but unremarkable | **Partial go.** Publish specification and process; lead proof with durability evidence and service instead of provenance. |
| One historic, resolved issue (e.g. a plant moved in 1998) | **Go, pre-empted.** Disclose it first, once, plainly, in the brand's own words, before anyone else finds it. Volunteered facts are inoculation; discovered facts are scandal. |
| Live or unresolved exposure | **No-go on transparency. Fix first.** The proof agenda shifts to Route C/D assets (people, place, service) and transparency is re-gated at 12 months. Publishing into an unresolved problem manufactures backlash #3 with our own hands. |

### 5.2 The product commitment — with carve-outs and legal review

A public pledge converts positioning into an operational asset. Written naïvely, it also creates warranty exposure and removes flexibility against input shortages, regulatory mandates and sustainability requirements.

**Drafting rules (legal sign-off required):**

- Commit to the **standard and the experience**, not to a frozen bill of materials: *"We will not change [hero]'s specification in any way a customer can detect, and we will never change it to reduce cost."*
- Named, pre-disclosed carve-outs: regulatory requirement, ingredient/material discontinuation, verified safety improvement, sustainability change that passes blind sensory/performance parity testing.
- **Governance mechanism:** any proposed hero change requires (a) blind parity testing against the current standard with a pre-agreed pass threshold, (b) Tier 1 sign-off, (c) proactive disclosure to the base *before* shelf, with reasoning. The commitment is that we will never do it quietly, not that we will never do it.
- Jurisdictional review for consumer-protection and advertising-code exposure; guarantee/repair pledges costed by finance before publication (§6.1).

### 5.3 Access engineering

Entry formats and price points for low-commitment trial; distribution in the channels the cohort uses (convenience, quick-commerce, relevant marketplaces, the right specialist retail); correct merchandising in those channels. Pricing architecture in §6.2; trade narrative in §6.3.

### 5.4 Occasion expansion

Based on the demand-space work, extend into 1–2 occasions the cohort has and the brand does not serve — under the architecture rules of §4.5.

### 5.5 Experience repair

Fix the mundane credibility-destroyers: mobile site speed, product pages, reviews, service response time, delivery, returns, parts availability. Under-35s judge modernity through operational competence long before advertising.

### 5.6 Loyalist engagement — commitment, framed as listening (not a change notice)

The earlier draft's "letter explaining what's changing" risks manufacturing the anxiety it aims to prevent: it creates a change narrative for a base that has noticed nothing, and hands trade press a story. Corrected approach:

- **Targeted, not broadcast.** Top-decile CRM buyers and engaged community members only. No press release, no public post.
- **Framed as commitment, not change.** The subject is what will *never* change. The spec commitment (§5.2) is the content.
- **Structured as a listening exercise.** A short "what must we never change?" panel of 200–500 heavy buyers, recruited before any external activity, consulted at each phase gate. Findings visibly acted on and reported back to them.
- **A named human channel** for concerns, answered inside 48 hours.
- **First access** to anything new — loyalists who feel consulted defend the brand; loyalists who feel surprised organise against it.

### 5.7 Internal engagement — before anything external

Staff cynicism leaks faster and further than advertising. Employee-led content (§7) is impossible without this.

| Audience | Activity | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Exec / board | Governance ratification: Immutables list, change budget, patience window, stop rules (§6.4, §9) | Phase 0, before Phase 1 spend |
| Marketing, insight, NPD, supply chain | Two-day working session on the evidence, not the idea. Everyone sees the same asset-test and demand-space data. Disagreement is resolved against data, not seniority. | Phase 0 |
| Sales / key accounts | Trade narrative training (§6.3) with retailer-facing proof, before any buyer conversation | Phase 1, ahead of range reviews |
| Manufacturing / long-tenure staff | "
